content: 1. The study by Sidney et al. (2007) in the British Journal of Haematology examined the combined effects of oral contraceptive use and prothrombotic mutations on thrombotic risk. 2. Sidney and colleagues (1998) conducted a pooled analysis of two U.S. studies to investigate the relationship between stroke and the use of low-dose oral contraceptives in young women, published in Stroke. 3. Sidney et al. (2004) explored the incidence of venous thromboembolic disease in users of low-estrogen combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives, as reported in Contraception. 4. A pooled analysis by Sidney et al. (2004) in Circulation assessed the risk of myocardial infarction associated with low-dose oral contraceptive use in young women. 5. Brunner Huber et al. (2006) conducted a case-cohort study in South Carolina to evaluate the impact of body mass index on the risk of oral contraceptive failure, published in Annals of Epidemiology. 6. Brunner Huber and Toth (2007) analyzed data from the 2002 National Survey of Family Growth to examine the relationship between obesity and oral contraceptive failure, as reported in the American Journal of Epidemiology. 7. Brunner and Hogue (2005) investigated the role of body weight in oral contraceptive failure using data from the 1995 National Survey of Family Growth, published in Annals of Epidemiology. 8. Burkman et al. (2009) studied the association between body weight or body mass index and the efficacy of two low-dose oral contraceptives, as reported in Contraception. 9. Dinger et al. (2011) compared the effectiveness of different progestogen regimens in a cohort study published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 10. Dinger et al. (2009) examined the effectiveness of oral contraceptives based on body mass index, weight, age, and other factors, as reported in the American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology. 11. Holt et al. (2002) investigated the relationship between body weight and the risk of oral contraceptive failure, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 12. Holt et al. (2005) further explored the impact of body mass index and weight on oral contraceptive failure risk, as reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 13. Jick et al. (2009) compared the risk of unintended pregnancies between users of contraceptive patches and oral contraceptives in the UK General Practice Research Database, published in Contraception. 14. Rubin et al. (2014) conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing the efficacy of a low-dose levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol patch versus a pill, as reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 15. McNicholas et al. (2013) studied contraceptive failures in overweight and obese users of combined hormonal contraceptives, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 16. Schramm and Schrah (2011) analyzed the efficacy and safety of an oral contraceptive containing chlormadinone acetate in non-interventional trials, as reported in Contraception. 17. Urdl et al. (2005) examined factors related to satisfaction with once-weekly transdermal contraception compared to oral contraception, published in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology. 18. Vessey (2001) reported findings from a large cohort study on oral contraceptive failures and body weight, published in the Journal of Family Planning and Reproductive Health Care. 19. Westhoff et al. (2012) found that body weight does not impact pregnancy rates during the use of a low-dose extended-regimen 91-day oral contraceptive, as reported in Contraception. 20. Zieman et al. (2002) analyzed pooled data on contraceptive efficacy and cycle control with the Ortho Evra/Evra transdermal system, published in Fertility and Sterility. 21. Heinemann et al. (1998) conducted a European case-control study on thromboembolic stroke in young women using oral contraceptives, published in Contraception. 22. The World Health Organization (1996) reported on the risk of hemorrhagic stroke and overall stroke associated with combined oral contraceptives in an international, multicenter case-control study, published in The Lancet. 23. The Collaborative Group for the Study of Stroke in Young Women (1975) examined oral contraceptives and stroke risk in young women, published in JAMA. 24. Croft and Hannaford (1989) identified risk factors for acute myocardial infarction in women, based on evidence from the Royal College of General Practitioners’ Oral Contraception Study, published in BMJ. 25. D’Avanzo et al. (1994) conducted an Italian case-control study on oral contraceptive use and myocardial infarction risk, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health. 26. Dunn et al. (1999) studied the risk of myocardial infarction in young female smokers, published in Heart. 27. Hannaford et al. (1994) reported on oral contraception and stroke risk using data from the Royal College of General Practitioners’ Oral Contraception Study, published in Stroke. 28. Kemmeren et al. (2002) conducted the RATIO study to assess the risk of ischemic stroke associated with oral contraceptives, published in Stroke. 29. Lidegaard (1995) examined the risk of cerebral thromboembolism in oral contraceptive users with diabetes, hypertension, migraine, or previous thrombotic disease, published in the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 30. Lubianica et al. (2003) identified oral contraceptives as a risk factor for uncontrolled blood pressure in hypertensive women, published in Contraception. 31. Narkiewicz et al. (1995) studied ambulatory blood pressure in mildly hypertensive women taking oral contraceptives, published in the American Journal of Hypertension. 32. Siritho et al. (2003) assessed the risk of ischemic stroke among oral contraceptive users in the Melbourne Risk Factor Study, published in Stroke. 33. Lubianica et al. (2005) demonstrated that stopping oral contraceptives effectively lowers blood pressure in hypertensive women, published in the Journal of Human Hypertension. 34. Carmichael et al.
